newsitem.title: CHINA: N.Korean Red Cross in Beijing for food aid talks.
newsitem.headline: N.Korean Red Cross in Beijing for food aid talks.

text.p: A North Korean Red Cross delegation arrived in Beijing on Saturday for the first inter- Korean Red Cross talks in almost five years that are aimed at speeding up food aid to the hungry North.
The talks were due to begin at a Beijing hotel later on Saturday and would focus on procedures for transporting and distributing food, but not the size or timing of aid, South Korean officials said.
The North Korean Red Cross delegation made no statements on arrival and it was not known how long the talks would last.

The South would seek assurances in the talks that food aid would not go to the North Korean army and would propose delivering food aid through the Korean border village of Panmunjom, instead of the present methods of using ships or trains through China, South Korean officials said.
The South also wanted to hand over aid directly to the North instead of through the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, the officials said.

International aid groups say North Korea, hit by devastating floods for two years in a row, is sliding into famine with reported deaths of children from malnutrition and farmers eating powdered wood to fill out their diet.
North Korea has said its food supplies would run out at the end of April.
The U.N. World Food Programme estimated there was only enough food to feed the country until June and then its 24 million people would have to wait for the next harvest in October and November.
The talks had been held up amid bickering between the two sides over where to hold the negotiations. The North insisted on Beijing while the South wanted talks in Panmunjom.
The last inter-Korean Red Cross talks were held in August, 1992 in Panmunjom, the only border crossing point between the two Koreas.
South Korea, the United States and Japan are scheduled to hold talks in Tokyo on May 7 to discuss food shortages in the North and ways to encourage the Stalinist hermit nation to join peace talks.
Seoul, Washington and Tokyo are worried that a desperate North Korean leadership might strike the South if an economic crisis threatened its survival.
Peace talks involving the two Koreas, the United States and China, are aimed at closing the book on the 1950-53 Korean War, which ended in a now-fraying armistice.
North Korea last month agreed to join four-nation peace talks if it was first guaranteed large-scale food aid, U.S. diplomatic recognition and an easing of trade sanctions.
Seoul and its allies agreed Pyongyang must not be allowed to use participation in the four-way talks as leverage to extract food assistance.
The United States has pledged $25 million and South Korea $6 million to the World Food Programme, which has appealed for $95.5 million to provide 203,000 tonnes of food to North Korea.
South Korea has said it was considering sending an additional 50,000 tonnes of corn.
Japan has held back food aid, partly due to anger over charges that North Korea kidnapped a Japanese schoolgirl in 1977 and spirited her to Pyongyang.
The United States has said it would not press Japan to donate more food aid to North Korea.
